exact_source_lines: We next show that $\equivrep{f}{} = \equivrep{g}{}$ is the \emph{least} upper bound on $S$. So let $j$ be any Cauchy sequence and suppose $\equivrep{j}{} < \equivrep{g}{}$. Reasoning as above (using the fact that $g$ is \emph{increasing}), there is $n \in \Nat$ such that $\equivrep{j}{} < (g(n))_\Real$. But by construction there is $h \in S$ such that $(g(n))_\Real \leq \equivrep{h}{}$, so $\equivrep{j}{} < \equivrep{h}{}$ and therefore $\equivrep{j}{}$ is not an upper bound on $S$.
